title: What is an SLO (Service Level Objective) — a target for reliability (e.g., 99.9% availability = max 8.7 hours downtime per year) — and what is an SLI (Service Level Indicator) — the actual measured metric (e.g., % of successful requests in last 30 days)?
shortTitle: What an SLO is and what an SLI is

s1_definition.profdef: A Service Level Indicator (SLI) is a precisely defined, measured quantity that reflects the quality of a service from the user's perspective, such as the percentage of successful requests or the percentage of requests served faster than a latency threshold over a window. A Service Level Objective (SLO) is a target value or range for an SLI over a period, for example 99.9 percent of requests successful over 30 days, which defines what "reliable enough" means. The SLI is the actual measurement; the SLO is the goal that measurement should meet, and together they turn reliability from a vague aspiration into a number you can track and act on.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine reliability as the punctuality of the branch. The SLI is the actual measurement — "out of every hundred customers this month, how many were served successfully and quickly?" The SLO is the promise the bank sets itself — "at least 99.9 out of every hundred must be served successfully." The SLI tells you how you are really doing; the SLO tells you how well you have decided you must do. If the measured number (SLI) stays at or above the target (SLO), the branch is meeting its reliability promise; if it drops below, the branch is failing its own standard and must act.
s1_definition.oneliner: An SLI is the actual measured quality of the service from the user's view, and an SLO is the target that SLI must meet — the measurement versus the goal.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Service Level Indicator (SLI) is a precisely defined, measured quantity that reflects the quality of a service from the user's perspective, such as the percentage of successful requests or the percentage of requests served faster than a latency threshold over a window. A Service Level Objective (SLO) is a target value or range for an SLI over a period, for example 99.9 percent of requests successful over 30 days, which defines what "reliable enough" means. The SLI is the actual measurement; the SLO is the goal that measurement should meet, and together they turn reliability from a vague aspiration into a number you can track and act on.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine reliability as the punctuality of the branch. The SLI is the actual measurement — "out of every hundred customers this month, how many were served successfully and quickly?" The SLO is the promise the bank sets itself — "at least 99.9 out of every hundred must be served successfully." The SLI tells you how you are really doing; the SLO tells you how well you have decided you must do. If the measured number (SLI) stays at or above the target (SLO), the branch is meeting its reliability promise; if it drops below, the branch is failing its own standard and must act.

**One line to remember:** An SLI is the actual measured quality of the service from the user's view, and an SLO is the target that SLI must meet — the measurement versus the goal.

sections.s2_technical:
An SLI is defined as a ratio of good events to total valid events, which keeps it between zero and one hundred percent and makes it directly comparable to a target. The most common SLIs are availability, measured as the proportion of successful requests out of all requests, and latency, measured as the proportion of requests served faster than a threshold such as 300 milliseconds. Other SLIs include error rate, throughput sufficiency, correctness, and freshness for data pipelines. The key discipline is that an SLI must reflect the user's experience, so you measure at the point closest to the user — for example at the load balancer or API gateway — and you define precisely what counts as a good event and what counts as valid, excluding things like health-check traffic that would distort the number.

An SLO is a target for an SLI over a defined window, usually a rolling period like 28 or 30 days. Saying the availability SLO is 99.9 percent means at least 99.9 percent of valid requests must succeed over that window. The choice of target matters enormously because each extra nine is dramatically more expensive: 99.9 percent allows about 8.76 hours of downtime per year, 99.99 percent allows about 52.6 minutes, and 99.999 percent allows about 5.26 minutes. So you set the SLO based on what users actually need and what the business can justify paying for, not at an arbitrary maximum, because chasing unnecessary nines wastes engineering effort that could deliver features.

The relationship between SLI and SLO is that the SLI is continuously measured and compared against the SLO to tell you whether the service is meeting its reliability goal. This naturally leads to an error budget, which is the amount of unreliability the SLO permits — if the SLO is 99.9 percent, the error budget is the remaining 0.1 percent of requests that may fail over the window. Teams use the error budget to make decisions: when there is budget remaining, they can take more deployment risk and ship features; when the budget is exhausted, they slow down and focus on reliability. This connects reliability targets to day-to-day engineering choices rather than leaving them abstract.

It is also important to distinguish an SLO from an SLA. An SLO is an internal target the team holds itself to, while a Service Level Agreement is an external contract with customers that often carries financial penalties if breached, and the SLA target is usually set looser than the internal SLO so the team has a safety margin — for example an internal SLO of 99.9 percent backing an SLA of 99.5 percent. A senior nuance is that SLIs should be chosen sparingly and meaningfully — a few SLIs that truly capture user happiness are better than many that do not — that you measure over user-centric windows rather than instantaneous spikes, and that you alert on burn rate, meaning how fast the error budget is being consumed, so you page a human only when the rate of failure threatens the SLO rather than on every transient blip.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India transfer API must be reliable. We want to define an availability SLI and a latency SLI, set SLOs for each, measure them over a window, and report whether each SLO is met along with the remaining error budget.

Problem 1 — "Is the transfer API reliable?" is unanswerable without a number. Defining availability as successful over total requests gives a concrete SLI.

Problem 2 — A number alone is not enough; we need a target. Setting the availability SLO at 99.9 percent and the latency SLO at 99 percent of requests under 300 milliseconds defines "reliable enough."

Problem 3 — We must know not just pass or fail but how much margin remains, to decide whether to keep shipping. Computing the error budget and how much is consumed drives that decision. Our runnable Java simulation records request outcomes, computes the availability and latency SLIs over a window, compares them to their SLOs, and reports the remaining error budget. Classes: `RequestOutcome`, `Sli`, `SloTarget`, `SloEvaluator`, and an `SloDemo` main.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a 30-day window of 10,000 transfer requests, with roughly five failures per ten thousand and about two percent of requests slower than 300 milliseconds.

Step 1 — The evaluator computes the availability SLI as successful requests over total. With about five failures in ten thousand, the SLI is about 99.95 percent, which is the actual measured quality of the service.

Step 2 — The evaluator compares the availability SLI to the availability SLO of 99.9 percent. Since 99.95 is at or above 99.9, the SLO is met, and the report notes how much of the 0.1 percent error budget has been consumed, leaving room to keep shipping features.

Step 3 — The evaluator computes the latency SLI as the proportion of requests served within 300 milliseconds. With about two percent slow, the SLI is about 98 percent.

Step 4 — The evaluator compares the latency SLI to the latency SLO of 99 percent. Since 98 is below 99, this SLO is breached, and the report flags that the error budget is over-consumed, signaling the team to freeze latency-risky features and fix performance.

Step 5 — The combined report shows the power of SLIs and SLOs: availability is comfortably meeting its target with budget to spare, while latency is failing its target, giving the team a precise, data-driven picture of exactly where reliability work is needed.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 03:00:00 [INFO   ] National Bank of India transfer-api — 30-day SLO report
2026-10-30 03:00:00 [INFO   ] availability SLI=99.950% >= SLO=99.900% → MET. Error budget consumed: 50.0% (room to ship).
2026-10-30 03:00:00 [SEVERE ] latency(<=300ms) SLI=98.000% < SLO=99.000% → BREACHED. Error budget consumed: 200.0% (freeze features, fix reliability).
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Service Level Indicator is a precisely defined, measured quantity that reflects the quality of a service from the user's point of view, and a Service Level Objective is the target that indicator must meet over a period. The SLI is the actual measurement — for example the percentage of successful requests, or the percentage of requests served faster than 300 milliseconds, over a rolling 30-day window — and the SLO is the goal, such as 99.9 percent of requests successful. So the simplest way I state it is that the SLI is how I am really doing and the SLO is how well I have decided I must do. I define an SLI as good events over valid events so it is a percentage directly comparable to the target, and I measure it as close to the user as possible, at the load balancer or gateway, excluding noise like health checks.

Choosing the SLO target matters because each additional nine is dramatically more expensive: 99.9 percent allows about 8.76 hours of downtime a year, 99.99 percent about 52 minutes, and 99.999 percent about five minutes. So I set the target based on what users actually need and what the business can justify, not at an arbitrary maximum, because chasing unnecessary nines wastes engineering effort. The SLI and SLO together naturally produce an error budget, which is the amount of unreliability the SLO permits — if the SLO is 99.9 percent the error budget is the remaining 0.1 percent — and teams use that budget to decide when to take deployment risk and ship features versus when to slow down and focus on reliability.

In my project at the National Bank of India we defined an availability SLI and a latency SLI for the transfer API, set the availability SLO at 99.9 percent and the latency SLO at 99 percent of requests under 300 milliseconds, and measured them over a 30-day window. In one report availability came in at about 99.95 percent, comfortably meeting its SLO with error budget to spare, while the latency SLI came in at about 98 percent, breaching its SLO, which told us precisely to freeze latency-risky changes and fix performance. A senior point I always add is that an SLO is an internal target while an SLA is an external contract usually set looser than the SLO for safety margin, that I keep SLIs few and genuinely user-centric, and that I alert on burn rate — how fast the error budget is being consumed — so a human is paged only when the SLO is truly threatened rather than on every transient blip.
